body:
That the validation is bypassed seems like a bug. The conversion form `1.9` to `1` and `0.9` to `0` is expected. To illustrate, have a look at the following irb session:

```
irb(main):001:0> 1.9.to_i
=> 1
irb(main):002:0> 0.9.to_i
=> 0
```

Also I am curious what is the reason to pass floats to an integer only field?

Yeah, that's why I say the truncation is understandable.  It seemed worth mentioning because it is a point where validations aren't super friendly to new (especially new to programming in general) developers.  

As for passing floats, really that's a matter of web user entry, in other words "who knows what they'll try?".

Certainly floats could be rounded to ints in a before_validation call if automatic rounding is desired instead of :only_integer's complaints--but at that point presumably someone knows enough to write their own custom validation.  And otherwise a call to :only_integer does the trick.

The main thing is that the current pitfall probably shouldn't exist.  And at least in my opinion the default behavior shouldn't lead to to_i truncation either, but that's certainly debatable.

Hey Pinbot,

This seems like a rather interesting bug to me. And I already have a pretty good idea how to fix it:

When the attribute is an integer and a float is passed in, remember to do the comparison with to_i. Then, if it fails, say something like:

```
Foo as an integer must be greater than 0
```

Are you planning on submitting a patch? I'd hate for double work to be done. If not, I'll take a stab and should be able to have a patch ready in a couple of days max.

I get the sense that you are much better poised to do a patch than I would
be, since I've not yet even looked at code that performs validations, so
I'd be happy to leave it to you.

Thanks!

> .
It would be interesting to hear what @rafaelfranca or @carlosantoniodasilva thinks about this bug. The problem is, that we already have the `:only_integer` option, which forces a `to_i` comparison.
According to the docs this should be validating by casting as a Float by default because `:only_integer` defaults to false.. shouldn't this work for comparing `0.9 > 0 #=> true`?

So, I've taken a lot longer than I should have working around this code. The problem is simply that you need to talk to the database to find out the column type to know whether a float to integer conversion is necessary. However, activemodel is supposed to be independent of the db, so any fix would go against the spirit of activemodel. I think the best case is to simply leave it be. Activemodel and activerecord are separate, so, in this case, what validates is different from what is entered into the db.

Well that spirit argument makes sense.  But you've got to admit that's a bit dodgy to able to validate (.2 > 0 ok) and save a record ( .2 becomes 0) and then when you call it up again later it's invalid (0 not > 0).  Some might find that vexing.

True. But, consider this: because of activerecord, in the last example:

``` ruby
x = BadValidation.new
x.foo = 0.9
x.foo #=> 0
```

Activerecord automatically changes the value to an int, so it's consistently confusing.

I didn't realize it was immediate like that.  That does help a little.  But
it's not the casting that bugs me so much as the idea that you shouldn't be
able to bypass validation without intending to.  From the example that you
just gave, I get the idea the the conversion happens before ever saving to
the database.  So I guess the 'talk to the database' happens even when
changing the 'in memory' object?  Which maybe opens the door to an argument
that having the 'talk' happen during validation wouldn't be that heinous?

On Tue, Apr 23, 2013 at 7:36 AM, Niel Malhotra notifications@github.comwrote:

> True. But, consider this: because of activerecord, in the last example:
> 
> x = BadValidation.newx.foo = 0.9x.foo #=> 0
> 
> Activerecord automatically changes the value to an int, so it's
> consistently confusing.
> 
> —
> Reply to this email directly or view it on GitHubhttps://github.com/rails/rails/issues/9957#issuecomment-16861842
> .

So, the conversion that happens is because of activerecord, which does talk to the database. So, when you call: ActiveRecordObject.new, It creates the object based on the table columns. However, activemodel, which takes care of validations, does not talk to the database ever (I'm 90 percent sure of this). So if you were to only include activemodel in your object and not activerecord, then you would not get this conversion.

I may be over simplifying the issue but it seems like you can do a pretty quick check if the `value` is a `Float` and the `option_value` is an `Integer` and then force `.to_i` on the value. The only edge case I'm encountering on that is that you need to handle infinity as it doesn't readily convert to an integer.

I wouldn't be extremely happy that a number which is about to be truncated is valid at one point in the lifecycle and then invalid at the next point. Perhaps that's the whole point of `only_integer: true`, and that I'm not aware of a number of significant edge cases.

So, the problem is whether the column in the database is a float or an integer. If the column in the db is a float, then we don't want to force the float to be an integer because it won't save invalid data. If the column in the db is an integer, then we want to force the float to be an integer. Knowing the column type requires digging into activerecord code which I am loathe to do as I explained above.

I do understand the reluctance.  What is the alternative to fixing?  I'm
thinking it would be to change the description of the save method to
something like "usually only saves if the record passes validation, but in
the event that the save to the database requires conversions then
validation may be bypassed"  If peeking at the database is expensive, then
I suppose it really isn't that unreasonable to have proper validation
behavior require conversion to the match column specifications, just so
long as there is something out there to make users aware of the requirement.

On one hand this starts to feel like making a mountain out of a molehill,
but on the other hand the whole "save only saves if the record is valid"
seems like a pretty fundamental rule so it sucks to leave a loophole.

On Wed, May 1, 2013 at 8:18 AM, Niel Malhotra notifications@github.comwrote:

> So, the problem is whether the column in the database is a float or an
> integer. If the column in the db is a float, then we don't want to force
> the float to be an integer because it won't save invalid data. If the
> column in the db is an integer, then we want to force the float to be an
> integer. Knowing the column type requires digging into activerecord code
> which I am loathe to do as I explained above.
> 
> —
> Reply to this email directly or view it on GitHubhttps://github.com/rails/rails/issues/9957#issuecomment-17286467
> .

I don't really believe this is an issue related to persistence though. What's going on here is an implicit comparison against a `Float` when that may or may not always be expected. There are really two options here:
- Keep the behavior the same way. Ensure the implicit `Float` conversion is well documented.
- Fix the code to ensure that behavior is different with the following situations behave differently:

``` rb
validates_numericaility_of :approved, greater_than: 0
```

and

``` rb
validates_numericality_of :approved, greater_than: 0.0
```

I'm actually somewhat surprised that these two cases have the same exact comparison. The behavior that I'd expect as a Ruby developer is that the first case is casting the left hand of the comparison as an `Integer` against our expected `greater_than: 0` and the latter case is ensuring that the left hand of the comparison is a `Float` against the `greater_than: 0.0`

The latter approach I'm sure breaks existing apps that are comfortable with the implicit `Float` coercion.

The behavior is actually pretty well documented. It's clearly stated that that when you say `greater_than: 0` that the `0` is coerced into `Kernal#float()`. While I don't love that the coercion is taking place; it's at least pretty clearly stated.

It's true the coercion is pretty clear when you look at the numericality
section.  Nonetheless, when I go back to the initial phenomenon, I'm still
pretty bothered by an invalid record getting saved without complaint by a
call that runs validations.  I mean the implication is that in order to be
properly testing, to account for the possibility that such an error has
slipped through somewhere, my tests should all make an extra call to valid?
after saving.  That seems...bad.

On Thu, May 2, 2013 at 7:18 PM, Patrick Robertson
notifications@github.comwrote:

> The behavior is actually pretty well documented. It's clearly stated that
> that when you say greater_than: 0 that the 0 is coerced into
> Kernal#float(). While I don't love that the coercion is taking place;
> it's at least pretty clearly stated.
>

> Reply to this email directly or view it on GitHubhttps://github.com/rails/rails/issues/9957#issuecomment-17375642

My two cents on this:

I think what you would like is a saner model of validation because Rubyists know what the difference is between `0` and `0.0`, but making this change will break validations for people. Probably a lot more people than your desired behavior fixes. I feel that the change will die as a pull request for the breaking behavior reason.

I can put a PR together if you feel strongly about it and see where it goes though.

I wouldn't want you to waste your time.  I hope I didn't come off as
insistent--I just felt at one point as though maybe the discussion of
causes had lost track of how weird the initial behavior is.

And I don't have a better idea, other than the notion of rechecking valid?
after saves.  That feels horrible even to do in tests (although that now
seems necessary). I certainly wouldn't propose it as baked-in behavior.

What lingers in my mind is 'if db behavior that happens after validation
can change a record to invalid after it is checked and before (or as) it is
saved, how do I know that this case we are looking at is the only way that
can happen?'  But nothing surefire (eg save a temp record to the database
and then delete unless it is valid) is without ugly costs and side effects.

issue.title: NumericalityValidator equal_to false positives with BigDecimal attributes
issue.body:
Given this model:

``` ruby
class Payment
  include ActiveModel::Model

  attr_accessor :amount

  validates :amount, numericality: {
    equal_to: ->(record) { record.amount }
  }
end
```

we should expect the numericality validation to always pass with a value for `amount`. However, it can fail if the amount column is a BigDecimal (which often happens as ActiveRecord represents `decimal` database columns with the BigDecimal type):

```
[7] pry(main)> payment = Payment.new amount: BigDecimal.new('706.06')
=> #<Payment:0x00000004c95c08 @amount=#<BigDecimal:4c95c58,'0.70606E3',18(18)>>
[8] pry(main)> payment.valid?
=> false
[9] pry(main)> payment.errors.to_a
=> ["Amount must be equal to 706.06"]
[10] pry(main)> payment.amount
=> #<BigDecimal:4c95c58,'0.70606E3',18(18)>
[11] pry(main)> payment.amount.to_f
=> 706.06
```

This appears to happen because NumericalityValidator takes the raw string value of :amount, and attempts to re-parse it to a Float: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/4-0-stable/activemodel/lib/active_model/validations/numericality.rb#L27

And as it turns out, ruby doesn't compare Float and BigDecimal reliably:

``` ruby
(0..9).each do |i|
  s = "706.0#{i}"
  puts s
  puts s.to_f == BigDecimal.new(s)
end
```

```
706.00
true
706.01
true
706.02
true
706.03
true
706.04
true
706.05
true
706.06
false
706.07
false
706.08
true
706.09
true
```

(output the same on 1.9.3 and 2.0.0-p247)

I haven't started trudging around the I'm not sure if this should be accepted under the general "Floats are imprecise", or if this is an actual ruby-core bug, but there are a few considerations:
1. Is it sensible to [always re-parse the values to a float](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/4-0-stable/activemodel/lib/active_model/validations/numericality.rb#L64), and arguably flakey type for comparisons?
2. If so, should we call `.to_f` on the `option_value` as well, so we're comparing the same types?
